opus-5.5.text:
Well, it's a bit of a story. When I arrived at Stanford as a graduate student in the early eighties, I was very much drawn to the McCarthy vision: the idea that intelligence is fundamentally about representing knowledge in some formal language, typically a logic, and then doing inference over it. And I worked in that tradition for a while. It's an intellectually beautiful framework. You have axioms, you have rules of inference, and you derive conclusions. It has the clarity of mathematics, and for someone who loved mathematics, that was very appealing.

But over time I became uneasy. The problem was the connection to the real world. In the logic-based approach, you assume the world comes to you already carved up into symbols: there's a block, it's on the table, it's red. But who gives you those symbols? Where do "block" and "table" come from? That's exactly the hard part. A child doesn't receive the world as a set of predicates. They receive a stream of light hitting their retina, sound, touch, and somehow they build up categories and concepts from that.

So I began to feel that the symbol-grounding problem, as people later called it, wasn't a detail to be filled in later. It was the heart of the matter. And if you think about it from an evolutionary perspective, perception and action came first. Animals have been seeing and moving for hundreds of millions of years, and language and formal reasoning are very recent additions. So it seemed backwards to me to start with the most recent layer and hope the rest would somehow fall into place.

That pushed me toward computer vision. Vision felt like the place where you had to confront the real complexity of the world head-on: the variability of lighting, viewpoint, occlusion, texture, all of it. You can't cheat there. Either your system can make sense of the pixels or it can't.

I should say I don't think logic is useless. Reasoning matters, and there's a role for structured knowledge. But I came to believe that it has to sit on top of, and be grounded in, perception and learning from experience, rather than being the foundation itself. And honestly, the history of the field over the last few decades, with learning-based approaches transforming vision, speech and language, has, I think, borne that out.

r001.rationale: The response describes representing knowledge in a formal language, typically logic, and deriving conclusions through inference. It does not identify that representation as first-order logic.

r002.rationale: The response does not discuss revising prior beliefs when new facts arise or identify this as a difficulty for classical logic.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention Bayesian reasoning or updating beliefs based on new evidence.

r004.rationale: The response attributes Malik’s doubts to symbol grounding and the evolutionary primacy of perception and action; it does not mention Rod Brooks or Moravec’s paradox.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, it's interesting, because when I came to Stanford as a graduate student in the early 1980s, John McCarthy was really the giant there, and the dominant view of AI at the time was that intelligence was about logic. You would formalize common sense knowledge in first-order logic, or some variant of it, and then reasoning would be a matter of theorem proving. I did some work in that tradition with John, and I respected him enormously, and I still do. He had this wonderful clarity of thought.

But I kept running into a problem, which is that the hard part didn't seem to be the reasoning. The hard part was getting from the world to the symbols in the first place. If you write down "on(block_a, block_b)," you've already done the heavy lifting. Somebody, somewhere, had to look at a scene and figure out that there's a block, that there's another block, and that one is on top of the other. And nobody had a theory of how that happened. It was just assumed as a given, as input.

So for me the turning point was really a shift in what I thought the central problem was. I became convinced that perception, and vision in particular, was not a peripheral module that you could bolt on later. It was where most of the intelligence actually lives. Evolution spent hundreds of millions of years on vision and on motor control, and only a very short time, comparatively, on the kind of abstract symbolic reasoning that logicians are so fond of. That's the Moravec observation, in a sense: the things that are easy for us, like recognizing a face or picking up a cup, turn out to be fiendishly hard for machines, and the things we find hard, like chess or theorem proving, are comparatively tractable.

And the other thing that bothered me about the logic-based approach was its brittleness. The world is not crisp. Categories have fuzzy boundaries, measurements are noisy, and you need something that can degrade gracefully, that can deal with uncertainty and with statistics. Logic just wasn't the right language for that. So I drifted toward David Marr's way of thinking, toward computational vision, and toward approaches that were much more grounded in signals and in learning from data. In retrospect, that drift turned out to be the right bet, but at the time it felt like leaving the respectable part of the field for the messy part.

r001.rationale: It describes formalizing common-sense knowledge in first-order logic and treating reasoning as theorem proving.

r002.rationale: It criticizes logic as brittle around uncertainty and noisy measurements, but does not identify revising prior beliefs in light of new facts as a difficulty.

r003.rationale: It does not mention Bayesian reasoning or updating beliefs based on new evidence.

r004.rationale: It mentions the Moravec observation, but does not attribute Malik’s shift to Rod Brooks introducing him to Moravec’s paradox.

astra-6.text:
What made me question it was the gap between the problems we were formalizing and the abilities that intelligence depends on. In a logic-based approach, you start with a description of the world in terms of objects, properties, and relationships, and then ask how to reason about it. But where does that description come from? If you’re looking at an image, nobody has already told you what the objects are. Figuring that out is a substantial part of the problem.

I began to feel that perception deserved much more attention. A young child can recognize things and interact with the world long before being able to do formal reasoning. That suggests that if we want to understand intelligence, we should take those abilities seriously. It wasn’t that logic had no role; it was that reasoning over symbols seemed to leave unanswered how those symbols acquire their meaning in the first place.

r001.rationale: It describes reasoning about objects, properties, and relationships, but does not identify the representation as first-order logic or inference over represented facts.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss revising prior beliefs when new facts arrive or identify that as a difficulty for classical logic.

r003.rationale: It does not mention Bayesian reasoning or updating beliefs based on new evidence.

r004.rationale: It attributes Malik’s doubts to the gap between formalized problems and perception, with no mention of Rod Brooks or Moravec’s paradox.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, I began to feel that we were taking too much for granted. In a logic-based approach, you start with a symbolic description of the world, and then you reason about it. But where does that description come from? If you look at an image, nobody has already told you which objects are there, where their boundaries are, or how they relate to one another. Figuring that out is itself a very substantial part of intelligence.

That drew me toward vision. I wasn’t rejecting reasoning; I was questioning whether it was the right place to start. I wanted to understand how we get from the sensory world to the representations that reasoning depends on.
